challenges.title: Password Hashing: Never Store Plaintext Passwords
description: One of the most critical security rules: never store plaintext passwords. Passwords must be hashed using a one-way cryptographic function before storage.

// Node.js with bcrypt (industry standard 2026) const bcrypt = require('bcrypt'); const SALT_ROUNDS = 12; // cost factor: higher = slower = more secure // Hashing (on registration) async function hashPassword(plaintext) { return bcrypt.hash(plaintext, SALT_ROUNDS); } // Verifying (on login) async function verifyPassword(plaintext, hash) { return bcrypt.compare(plaintext, hash); } // Why NOT to use MD5/SHA1: // 'password123' -> MD5 -> '482c811da5d5b4bc6d497ffa98491e38' // Rainbow tables instantly crack common MD5 hashes! // bcrypt adds a unique salt + is computationally expensive by design
Modern password hashing algorithms: bcrypt (most common), Argon2 (winner of Password Hashing Competition, recommended for new apps), scrypt (memory-hard, used by many cryptocurrencies).
A salt is random data added before hashing to ensure identical passwords produce different hashes, defeating pre-computed rainbow table attacks.
Instructions

Implement a simple (non-cryptographic) password strength validator checkPasswordStrength that returns 'weak', 'medium', or 'strong' based on: length >= 8 required, strong requires >= 12 chars AND uppercase AND lowercase AND number AND special char.
challengeSeed: // strong: >= 12 chars AND all four character types
tests: assert(checkPasswordStrength('abc') === 'weak', 'message: Passwords shorter than 8 chars should be weak.');
assert(checkPasswordStrength('Str0ng!Pass#2026') === 'strong', 'message: >= 12 chars with all types should be strong.');

challenges.title: XSS Prevention: Sanitizing User Input
description: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is one of the most common web vulnerabilities. It occurs when an attacker injects malicious scripts into content served to other users.

// XSS Attack Example: // User submits: <script>document.cookie</script> // App displays it unescaped in HTML // Every visitor's browser executes the script! // Prevention: HTML entity encoding function escapeHTML(str) { return str .replace(/&/g, '&') .replace(//g, '>') .replace(/"/g, '"') .replace(/'/g, '''); } // <script> is displayed as text, not executed escapeHTML('<script>alert(1)</script>'); // Outputs: '<script>alert(1)</script>'

Types of XSS: Stored XSS (injected content saved to DB, served to all users), Reflected XSS (payload in URL parameter reflected back), DOM-based XSS (client-side script writes unsanitized data to DOM).
Modern defenses: Content-Security-Policy headers, React/Vue automatic escaping, textContent instead of innerHTML, input validation libraries like DOMPurify.
Instructions
Implement escapeHTML that converts the five dangerous characters (&, <, >, ", ') to their HTML entity equivalents, preventing XSS when displaying user content.
challengeSeed: // Order matters: & must be replaced first!
tests: assert(escapeHTML('"quoted"') === '"quoted"', 'message: Double quotes should be escaped.');
assert(escapeHTML('a & b') === 'a & b', 'message: Ampersand should be escaped.');
assert(escapeHTML("it's") === 'it's', 'message: Single quotes should be escaped.');

challenges.title: JWT Authentication: Stateless Identity Tokens
description: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are the standard for stateless authentication in 2026 REST APIs and SPAs. A JWT contains a header, payload (claims), and signature — all base64-encoded and dot-separated.

// JWT structure: header.payload.signature // eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJ1c2VySWQiOjEsInJvbGUiOiJ1c2VyIn0.signature // Node.js with jsonwebtoken const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken'); const SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET; // Sign (create token) const token = jwt.sign( { userId: 1, role: 'admin' }, // payload SECRET, { expiresIn: '24h' } // options ); // Verify try { const decoded = jwt.verify(token, SECRET); console.log(decoded.userId); // 1 } catch (err) { // TokenExpiredError or JsonWebTokenError res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid token' }); }
JWT best practices: use short expiry (<24h) + refresh tokens, store in httpOnly cookies (not localStorage) to prevent XSS theft, validate on every request, include only necessary claims in payload.
Instructions

Implement a simplified token system: createToken(payload, secret) returns a base64-encoded token string, and verifyToken(token, secret) decodes and returns the payload, or returns null if the secret doesn't match.
tests: var token = createToken({userId: 1, role: 'admin'}, 'mysecret'); assert(typeof token === 'string' && token.includes('.'), 'message: Token should be a string with a dot separator.');
var payload = verifyToken(token, 'mysecret'); assert(payload && payload.userId === 1, 'message: verifyToken should decode the userId.');
assert(verifyToken(token, 'wrongsecret') === null, 'message: Wrong secret should return null.');
assert(verifyToken('invalid.token', 'mysecret') === null, 'message: Tampered token should return null.');

challenges.title: Rate Limiting: Protecting APIs from Abuse
description: Rate limiting restricts how many requests a client can make in a time window, protecting against brute-force attacks, DoS, scraping, and API abuse.

// Express rate limiter (express-rate-limit) const rateLimit = require('express-rate-limit'); const loginLimiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, // 15 minutes max: 10, // max 10 login attempts per 15 min message: { error: 'Too many login attempts, try again later' }, standardHeaders: true, // Return limit info in RateLimit-* headers legacyHeaders: false }); app.post('/login', loginLimiter, loginHandler); // Different limits for different endpoints: // Public API: 100 req/min // Auth endpoints: 10 req/15min (brute force protection) // AI endpoints: 20 req/min (expensive inference)

Rate limiting strategies: fixed window (reset counter every N seconds), sliding window (rolling N-second lookback), token bucket (tokens replenish over time), leaky bucket (queue-based, smooths bursts).
Instructions

Implement a fixed window rate limiter factory function. createRateLimiter(maxRequests, windowMs) returns a function that takes a clientId. It returns true if the request is allowed, false if rate limited.
challengeSeed: // Increment count; return false if over limit
tests: var limiter = createRateLimiter(3, 60000); assert(limiter('user1') === true, 'message: First request should be allowed.'); assert(limiter('user1') === true, 'message: Second request should be allowed.'); assert(limiter('user1') === true, 'message: Third request should be allowed.');
assert(limiter('user1') === false, 'message: Fourth request should be rate limited.');
assert(limiter('user2') === true, 'message: A different client should have its own counter.');
